lessons.title: Propositional logic
lessons.summary: Propositions, connectives and truth tables, why "if p then q" behaves the way it does, the equivalences you use to simplify conditions, and valid versus invalid arguments.
lessons.body:
Every `if` statement you have written is a small piece of logic. Propositional logic is the precise version of that: a way of combining true/false statements and working out, mechanically, when the combination is true.

It is the foundation for everything else in this module. Proofs are built from it, predicate logic extends it, and the SAT problem in the last lesson asks one question about it that turns out to be enormously hard and enormously useful.

## Propositions

In the classical two-valued logic used here, a proposition is a statement that is either true or false, never both.

- "7 is prime" is a proposition (true).
- "2 + 2 = 5" is a proposition (false).
- "x > 3" is **not** a proposition on its own: its truth depends on what the unknown x is. (Predicate logic, next lesson, handles this.)
- "Close the door" is not a proposition: it is neither true nor false.

We name propositions with letters: p, q, r. These are **propositional variables**, the logical equivalent of Boolean variables in code. When we write down the truth values themselves, T means true and F means false.

## The connectives

Five connectives build bigger formulas from smaller ones. Each has its own symbol, and these symbols appear in every lesson of this module, so it is worth learning them now.

```formula
¬p
p ∧ q
p ∨ q
p → q
p ↔ q
where
p, q: propositions (propositional variables), each either true or false
¬: NOT (negation). ¬p is true exactly when p is false
∧: AND (conjunction). p ∧ q is true only when both p and q are true
∨: OR (disjunction). p ∨ q is true when at least one of p, q is true, including when both are
→: IMPLIES (implication, the conditional). p → q reads "if p then q", and is false only when p is true and q is false
↔: IF AND ONLY IF (the biconditional). p ↔ q is true when p and q have the same truth value, both true or both false
In words: "not p", "p and q", "p or q", "if p then q" and "p if and only if q": the five ways to build a bigger statement out of p and q.
```

The table gives each one's name and the nearest Python.

| Symbol | Name | Read as | Python |
|---|---|---|---|
| ¬p | negation | not p | `not p` |
| p ∧ q | conjunction | p and q | `p and q` |
| p ∨ q | disjunction | p or q | `p or q` |
| p → q | implication | if p then q | `(not p) or q` |
| p ↔ q | biconditional | p if and only if q | `p == q` |

The Python column assumes Boolean operands. Python and/or return operands and short-circuit; arbitrary objects can have custom truth tests and equality. The logical connectives have their meaning fixed by a **truth table**, which lists every combination of inputs, one per row. Each variable doubles the number of combinations, because every existing row splits into a "true" version and a "false" version:

```formula
N_rows = 2^n
N_rows = 2^2 = 4   for n = 2
N_rows = 2^3 = 8   for n = 3
where
N_rows: the number of rows in the truth table, one per combination of input values
n: the number of propositional variables in the formula
2^n: n copies of 2 multiplied together (2 to the power n)
In words: a truth table over n variables has 2 to the power n rows, so two variables need 4 rows and three need 8.
```

Here is the truth table for all five connectives over p and q. T is true and F is false; each column is one connective.

```
p q | ¬p  p∧q  p∨q  p→q  p↔q
----+-------------------------
T T |  F   T    T    T    T
T F |  F   F    T    F    F
F T |  T   F    T    T    F
F F |  T   F    F    T    T
```

Two things trip people up.

- **∨ is inclusive.** p ∨ q is true when both are true. "Exclusive or" (exactly one) is a separate connective, written ⊕. In Python on booleans it is `p != q`.
- **→ is false in exactly one row**: when p is true and q is false.

Exclusive or is "not (p if and only if q)", because it is true exactly when p and q differ:

```formula
p ⊕ q ≡ ¬(p ↔ q)
where
p, q: propositions, each true or false
⊕: XOR (exclusive or): true when exactly one of p, q is true
↔: if and only if: true when p and q have the same truth value
¬: NOT: flips true to false and false to true
≡: is logically equivalent to: the two sides have the same truth value in every row of the truth table
In words: "exactly one of p and q" means the same as "it is not the case that p and q agree". With p true and q false, both sides are true.
```

## Why implication works this way

The bottom two rows of p → q surprise everyone. Why is "if p then q" true whenever p is false? Here is the rule in one place:

```formula
p → q = F   when p = T and q = F
p → q = T   otherwise
where
p: the "if" part (the premise or antecedent), a proposition; here "you pass the exam"
q: the "then" part (the conclusion or consequent), a proposition; here "I buy you dinner"
→: implies: "if p then q"
T: true
F: false
In words: an implication is broken only by a true premise with a false conclusion; in the other three rows it holds.
```

Think of p → q as a **promise**. "If you pass the exam, I'll buy you dinner." The only way I break the promise is if you pass (p true) and I don't buy dinner (q false). If you fail, I have kept my word whatever I do. A promise that was never triggered was never broken.

This is called **vacuous truth**, and it matters. "Every element of the empty list is negative" is true, because there is no element to break it. Python agrees: `all([])` is `True`.

The connective defined by this table is the **material conditional**. It says nothing about cause. "If 2 + 2 = 5 then the Moon is cheese" is true, because the premise is false. That feels wrong in English, but it is the definition that makes proofs work.

> [!tip] Reading p → q
> All of these mean p → q: "if p then q", "p implies q", "p only if q", "q if p", "p is sufficient for q", "q is necessary for p". The phrase "p only if q" catches people out: it means p cannot happen without q, which is p → q, not q → p.

## Converse, inverse, contrapositive

From an implication p → q you can form three related statements by swapping the two sides, negating both, or doing both:

```formula
p → q
q → p
¬p → ¬q
¬q → ¬p
where
p → q: the original implication, "if p then q"
q → p: the converse: the two sides swapped
¬p → ¬q: the inverse: both sides negated
¬q → ¬p: the contrapositive: swapped and negated
p, q: propositions, each true or false
¬: NOT: ¬p is true exactly when p is false
→: implies: false only when the left side is true and the right side is false
In words: the original, its converse, its inverse and its contrapositive. Only the contrapositive always has the same truth table as the original.
```

| Name | Form | Same as p → q? |
|---|---|---|
| Contrapositive | ¬q → ¬p | Yes, always |
| Converse | q → p | Not in general |
| Inverse | ¬p → ¬q | Not in general |

"If it is raining, the ground is wet" does not mean "if the ground is wet, it is raining" (a sprinkler could be on). That is the converse, and assuming it is one of the most common reasoning errors in proofs, code reviews and incident postmortems.

The contrapositive, "if the ground is not wet, it is not raining", is equivalent. You can check by truth table: both are false in exactly one row: p true and q false. The converse and the inverse are equivalent to *each other* (one is the contrapositive of the other).

## Tautologies, contradictions, satisfiable formulas

Tautology, contradiction and contingency form three disjoint classes. Satisfiability is a related property that overlaps them. The two simplest examples, "p or not p" and "p and not p":

```formula
p ∨ ¬p ≡ T
p ∧ ¬p ≡ F
where
p: a proposition, true or false
¬: NOT: ¬p is true exactly when p is false
∨: OR: true when at least one side is true
∧: AND: true only when both sides are true
≡: is logically equivalent to: same truth value in every row
T: the constant "true", a formula that is true in every row
F: the constant "false", a formula that is false in every row
In words: "p or not p" is true whatever p is, and "p and not p" is false whatever p is. Try p = T and p = F: the first gives T both times, the second F both times.
```

- A **tautology** is true in every row. Example: p ∨ ¬p.
- A **contradiction** is false in every row. Example: p ∧ ¬p.
- A **contingent formula** is true in some rows and false in others.
- A formula is **satisfiable** if at least one row makes it true: both tautologies and contingent formulas qualify.

These are linked: a formula A is a tautology exactly when its negation ¬A is unsatisfiable. SAT solvers exploit this to check that something *always* holds: they search for a row where it fails, and "no such row" is a proof.

## Logical equivalence

Two formulas are **logically equivalent** if they have the same truth value in every row:

```formula
A ≡ B
where
A, B: any two formulas built from propositions and connectives
≡: is logically equivalent to: A and B have the same truth value in every row of their truth table
In words: A and B always agree. Equivalently, the formula "A if and only if B" is a tautology.
```

These are the laws you use daily to simplify conditions. Each line can be checked with a four- or eight-row truth table.

```formula
¬¬p ≡ p
¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q
¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q
p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q
p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p
p ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r)
p ∨ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r)
p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p
p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p)
where
p, q, r: propositions, each true or false
¬: NOT: flips true and false; ¬¬p is NOT applied twice
∧: AND: true only when both sides are true
∨: OR (inclusive): true when at least one side is true
→: implies: false only when the left side is true and the right side false
↔: if and only if: true when both sides have the same truth value
≡: is logically equivalent to: same truth value in every row
In words: line by line, these are double negation, De Morgan's two laws, the implication law, the contrapositive, distribution of AND over OR and of OR over AND, absorption, and the biconditional law.
```

**De Morgan's laws** are the ones you will use most: to negate an AND, negate each part and switch to OR (and vice versa).

Commutativity (order doesn't matter), associativity (grouping doesn't matter) and the identity laws complete the toolkit:

```formula
p ∧ T ≡ p
p ∨ T ≡ T
p ∨ F ≡ p
p ∧ F ≡ F
where
p: a proposition, true or false
T: the constant true
F: the constant false
∧: AND: true only when both sides are true
∨: OR: true when at least one side is true
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: AND with true and OR with false change nothing; OR with true is always true and AND with false is always false.
```

> [!example] Simplifying a guard
> A code review finds `if not (user.banned or not user.verified):`. Write b for `user.banned` and v for `user.verified`, then apply De Morgan and double negation, as shown below.

```formula
¬(b ∨ ¬v) ≡ ¬b ∧ ¬¬v
          ≡ ¬b ∧ v
where
b: the proposition "the user is banned"
v: the proposition "the user is verified"
¬: NOT; ¬¬v is NOT applied twice, which gives v back
∨: OR: true when at least one side is true
∧: AND: true only when both sides are true
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: "not (banned or unverified)" is the same as "not banned and verified". The first step is De Morgan, the second is double negation.
```

So it is `if not user.banned and user.verified:`, which reads far better.

You can also prove an equivalence algebraically, one law per step. Here is a derivation that tells you exactly when an implication fails:

```formula
¬(p → q) ≡ ¬(¬p ∨ q)
         ≡ ¬¬p ∧ ¬q
         ≡ p ∧ ¬q
where
p, q: propositions, each true or false
¬: NOT: flips true and false
→: implies: "if p then q"
∨: OR: true when at least one side is true
∧: AND: true only when both sides are true
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: an implication is false exactly when p is true and q is false. The steps use the implication law, then De Morgan, then double negation.
```

## Checking equivalence in code

With n variables there are only 2ⁿ rows, so a computer can check any equivalence by brute force.

```python
from itertools import product

def equivalent(f, g, n):
    for v in product([False, True],
                     repeat=n):
        if f(*v) != g(*v):
            return False, v
    return True, None

imp = lambda p, q: (not p) or q
contra = lambda p, q: imp(not q, not p)
conv = lambda p, q: imp(q, p)

print(equivalent(imp, contra, 2))
print(equivalent(imp, conv, 2))
```

The output is `(True, None)` then `(False, (False, True))`. The second line hands you a counterexample: with p false and q true, p → q is true but its converse q → p is false.

How far does brute force go? Count the rows:

```formula
N_rows = 2^n
N_rows = 2^20 = 1,048,576   for n = 20
N_rows = 2^60 ≈ 1.15 × 10^18   for n = 60
where
N_rows: the number of rows (assignments) to check
n: the number of propositional variables
2^n: n copies of 2 multiplied together
≈: approximately equal to
10^18: a 1 followed by 18 zeros (a billion billion)
In words: 20 variables is about a million rows, which takes a laptop well under a second, but 60 variables is over a billion billion rows, far too many to check one by one.
```

This works for 10 or 20 variables. At 60 variables brute force is hopeless. That gap is the subject of the SAT lesson.

## Precedence

By convention, ¬ binds tightest, then ∧, then ∨, then →, then ↔. Implication is usually read right-associatively (grouped from the right):

```formula
¬p ∧ q → r   means   ((¬p) ∧ q) → r
p → q → r    means   p → (q → r)
where
p, q, r: propositions, each true or false
¬: NOT: applies only to the thing directly after it
∧: AND: binds more tightly than → (it is grouped first)
→: implies: binds more loosely than ¬ and ∧
In words: NOT is applied first, then AND, then OR, then implication; a chain of implications groups from the right.
```

Python follows the same order for `not`, `and`, `or`. When in doubt, add brackets: other people will read the code too.

## Valid arguments

An **argument** has premises and a conclusion. It is **logically valid** if the conclusion is true in every row where all the premises are true. Equivalently:

```formula
(P_1 ∧ P_2 ∧ ... ∧ P_k) → C ≡ T
where
P_1, P_2, ..., P_k: the k premises, each a formula
C: the conclusion, a formula
k: the number of premises
...: "and so on", the premises in between
∧: AND: true only when every part is true
→: implies: false only when the left side is true and the right side false
≡: is logically equivalent to
T: the constant true, so "≡ T" means "is a tautology"
In words: an argument is valid exactly when "if all the premises hold then the conclusion holds" is true in every row.
```

The standard valid forms, written with ⊢ ("therefore"):

```formula
p → q, p ⊢ q
p → q, ¬q ⊢ ¬p
p → q, q → r ⊢ p → r
p ∨ q, ¬p ⊢ q
p ∨ q, p → r, q → r ⊢ r
where
p, q, r: propositions, each true or false
,: separates the premises
⊢: "therefore": the formula on the right follows validly from the premises on the left. (Strictly ⊢ means "can be derived by the rules of a proof system", and ∴ is the usual "therefore" sign; for classical propositional logic the soundness and completeness theorems make ⊢ coincide with "true in every row where the premises are true", which is written ⊨)
→: implies
¬: NOT
∨: OR (inclusive)
In words: line by line, modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical syllogism, disjunctive syllogism and proof by cases (disjunction elimination).
```

| Rule | Premises | Conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| Modus ponens | p → q, p | q |
| Modus tollens | p → q, ¬q | ¬p |
| Hypothetical syllogism | p → q, q → r | p → r |
| Disjunctive syllogism | p ∨ q, ¬p | q |
| Proof by cases | p ∨ q, p → r, q → r | r |

And two famous invalid ones:

- **Affirming the consequent**: from p → q and q, conclude p. Invalid (row p = F, q = T).
- **Denying the antecedent**: from p → q and ¬p, conclude ¬q. Invalid (same row).

```formula
p → q, q ⊬ p
p → q, ¬p ⊬ ¬q
where
p, q: propositions, each true or false
→: implies
¬: NOT
⊬: "does not follow": some row makes every premise true and the conclusion false
In words: knowing the "then" part is true doesn't tell you the "if" part, and knowing the "if" part is false doesn't tell you the "then" part. The row p = F, q = T breaks both.
```

> [!warning] Debugging with the converse
> "If the cache is down, latency spikes. Latency spiked, so the cache is down." That is affirming the consequent. Latency spikes have many causes. Modus tollens is the safe direction: "latency did not spike, so the cache is not down" (given the premise holds).

Validity is about form, not truth. "If pigs fly, I am the Queen; pigs fly; so I am the Queen" is valid. Its conclusion is false only because a premise is false. An argument that is valid *and* has true premises is called a **sound argument**.

## How many connectives do you need?

Not five. Implication and the biconditional can be rewritten with the others, and OR can be rewritten with NOT and AND:

```formula
p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q
p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p)
p ∨ q ≡ ¬(¬p ∧ ¬q)
where
p, q: propositions, each true or false
¬: NOT
∧: AND: true only when both sides are true
∨: OR: true when at least one side is true
→: implies
↔: if and only if
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: anything written with → and ↔ can be rewritten with NOT, AND and OR, and by De Morgan OR itself can be written with NOT and AND.
```

So the set {¬, ∧, ∨} can express every truth table, and even {¬, ∧} alone suffices. A set like this is **functionally complete**.

Remarkably, a single connective is enough: **NAND** ("not and"), written ↑. Feeding a value into both inputs of a NAND negates it, which is the key to building the rest:

```formula
p ↑ q ≡ ¬(p ∧ q)
¬p ≡ p ↑ p
p ∧ q ≡ (p ↑ q) ↑ (p ↑ q)
p ∨ q ≡ (p ↑ p) ↑ (q ↑ q)
where
p, q: propositions, each true or false
↑: NAND (not and): false only when both sides are true
¬: NOT
∧: AND
∨: OR
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: NAND is "not both". NAND of a value with itself is its negation; NAND of a NAND gives AND back; NAND of two negations gives OR (by De Morgan).
```

Check the AND line with p = T and q = T: p ↑ q is F, and F ↑ F is T, which matches p ∧ q.

This is why chips can be built from NAND gates alone. NOR is also complete on its own; AND, OR and NOT individually are not.

## Key takeaways
- A proposition is true or false; connectives combine them, and a truth table with 2ⁿ rows (n variables) defines any formula's meaning.
- p → q is false only when p is true and q is false; when p is false it is vacuously true.
- The contrapositive ¬q → ¬p is always equivalent to p → q; converse and inverse are not equivalent to it in general.
- De Morgan, implication-as-disjunction and distribution let you simplify conditions safely.
- An argument is valid when the conclusion holds in every row where the premises do; affirming the consequent is the classic fallacy.
- {¬, ∧} and NAND alone are functionally complete.

questions.prompt:
A function's docstring promises: "If the input list is sorted, the output list is sorted." You call it with an **unsorted** list and get an unsorted list back. Has the promise (read as p → q) been broken?

*Symbols: → means "implies" (if ... then).*

options.text: Yes: the output is unsorted, so q is false and the implication is false
options.explanation: This ignores p. An implication is only false when p is true *and* q is false. Here p (input sorted) is false.

options.text: No: p is false, so p → q is true whatever the output is
options.explanation: Correct. With a false premise the implication is vacuously true. The docstring made no promise about unsorted inputs.

options.text: It cannot be decided without knowing whether the function sorts
options.explanation: The truth value of p → q depends only on the truth values of p and q, not on how the function works internally. Both are known here.

options.text: Yes: an implication requires that q is false whenever p is false
options.explanation: That describes the inverse ¬p → ¬q, which is not equivalent to p → q. Reading the inverse into a promise is a classic error.

questions.workedExample:
1. Let p be "the input is sorted" and q be "the output is sorted".
2. Here p is false and q is false.
3. Apply the rule for implication:

```formula
p → q = F   when p = T and q = F
p → q = T   otherwise
p → q = T   as p = F and q = F
where
p: the premise, "the input list is sorted"; false in this call
q: the conclusion, "the output list is sorted"; false in this call
→: implies: "if p then q"
T: true
F: false
¬: NOT, used in option D: ¬p → ¬q ("if not p then not q") is the inverse, a different statement
In words: the promise is broken only by a sorted input that comes back unsorted. An unsorted input cannot break it, whatever comes out.
```

The full truth table, with the rows marked:

```
p q | p→q
T T |  T
T F |  F   <- only failing row
F T |  T
F F |  T   <- our case
```

4. The promise is broken only by a sorted input that produces an unsorted output. An unsorted input cannot break it.

questions.prompt: Your team's rule is: "If a pull request is merged, then CI passed." Which statement is **logically equivalent** to this rule?

options.text: If CI passed, then the pull request is merged
options.explanation: That is the converse (q → p). It is not equivalent: CI can pass on a PR nobody has merged yet.

options.text: If the pull request is not merged, then CI did not pass
options.explanation: That is the inverse (¬p → ¬q). It is equivalent to the converse, not to the original rule.

options.text: If CI did not pass, then the pull request is not merged
options.explanation: Correct. This is the contrapositive (¬q → ¬p), which is always equivalent to p → q.

options.text: The pull request is merged and CI passed
options.explanation: That is p ∧ q, a much stronger claim. The rule does not assert that any PR is actually merged.

questions.workedExample:
1. Let p be "the PR is merged" and q be "CI passed". The rule is p → q.
2. Form the variants by swapping and negating:

```formula
p → q
q → p
¬p → ¬q
¬q → ¬p
where
p: "the pull request is merged"
q: "CI passed"
p → q: the rule itself, "if merged then CI passed"
q → p: the converse (sides swapped)
¬p → ¬q: the inverse (both sides negated)
¬q → ¬p: the contrapositive (swapped and negated)
¬: NOT: true exactly when the statement after it is false
→: implies: false only when the left side is true and the right side is false
∧: AND, used in option D: p ∧ q is true only when both are true
In words: the rule, its converse, its inverse and its contrapositive. Only the contrapositive always agrees with the rule.
```

3. Check the contrapositive against p → q row by row. Both are false only when p is true and q is false (merged, CI failed), and true otherwise.
4. So the contrapositive is the equivalent one. "CI did not pass, so it cannot have been merged" is just the rule read backwards correctly.

questions.prompt: A service has 6 independent boolean feature flags. To test a condition over them exhaustively, you build its truth table. How many rows does it have?

options.explanation: That is 2 × 6, as if each flag contributed two rows independently. Rows multiply, they don't add.
That is 6², which counts something else. Each flag doubles the number of combinations, so the count is a power of 2.
Correct. Each of the 6 flags is T or F independently, giving 2⁶ = 64 combinations.
That is 6! (orderings of the flags). A truth table cares about values, not order.

questions.workedExample:
1. One flag: 2 rows (true, false).
2. Each extra flag doubles the rows, because every existing row splits into a true and a false version.
3. Count for 6 flags:

```formula
N_rows = 2^n
N_rows = 2^6 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2
N_rows = 64   for n = 6
N_rows = 2^40 ≈ 1.1 × 10^12   for n = 40
where
N_rows: the number of rows in the truth table, one per combination of flag values
n: the number of independent boolean flags
2^n: n copies of 2 multiplied together
≈: approximately equal to
10^12: a 1 followed by 12 zeros (a million million)
In words: 6 flags give 64 combinations. Each flag doubles the count, so 40 flags would give about 1.1 million million rows.
```

4. This doubling is why brute force works for small n but not for large n. (The wrong options: 2 × 6 = 12 adds instead of multiplying, 6² = 36 squares the count, and 6! = 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 720 counts orderings of the flags.)

questions.prompt:
Simplify this guard, where `a` and `b` are booleans:

```python
if not (a and not b):
    ...
```

options.explanation: This negates each part but forgets to flip `and` to `or`. De Morgan's law changes the connective as well as negating the parts.
This flips `and` to `or` but fails to cancel the double negation on b: ¬¬b is b, not ¬b.
This drops the negation on a altogether. Check a true, b false: the original is false, but `a or b` is true.
Correct. By De Morgan and double negation, `not (a and not b)` becomes `not a or b`, which is also "if a then b".

questions.workedExample:
Write the guard in logic symbols, then apply the laws one at a time:

```formula
¬(a ∧ ¬b) ≡ ¬a ∨ ¬¬b
          ≡ ¬a ∨ b
          ≡ a → b
where
a, b: the boolean variables `a` and `b`, each true or false
¬: NOT (Python `not`); ¬¬b is NOT applied twice, which gives b back
∧: AND (Python `and`): true only when both sides are true
∨: OR (Python `or`): true when at least one side is true
→: implies: false only when the left side is true and the right side false
≡: is logically equivalent to: same truth value for every input
In words: "not (a and not b)" becomes "not a or b" by De Morgan and then double negation, which is also "if a then b".
```

Check the one row where it should be false, a true and b false:

```formula
¬(T ∧ ¬F) = ¬(T ∧ T) = ¬T = F
¬T ∨ F = F ∨ F = F
where
T: true
F: false
¬: NOT
∧: AND
∨: OR
In words: with a true and b false, the original guard and the simplified one are both false.
```

They agree, and the other three rows are true for both.

questions.prompt:
Which of these formulas are **tautologies** (true in every row)? Select all that apply.

*Symbols: ¬ means NOT; ∧ means AND; ∨ means OR (inclusive); → means "implies" (if ... then).*

options.explanation: Correct. If q is true, p → q is true. If q is false, q → p is true. Either way one disjunct holds.
Not a tautology. It assumes an implication gives you its converse. In the row p false, q true, p → q is true but q → p is false, so the whole formula is false.
Correct. This is modus ponens written as a formula: whenever both premises are true, q is true.
Not a tautology. This is affirming the consequent. Row p = F, q = T makes both premises true and the conclusion false.
Correct. The premise p ∧ ¬p is false in every row, so the implication is vacuously true everywhere. From a contradiction, anything follows.

questions.workedExample:
The symbols used in the options:

```formula
p → q
(p → q) ∧ p
p ∧ ¬p
where
p, q: propositions, each true (T) or false (F)
→: implies: false only when the left side is true and the right side false
∧: AND: true only when both sides are true
∨: OR: true when at least one side is true
¬: NOT: ¬p is true exactly when p is false
T: true
F: false
In words: an implication can only fail with a true left side and a false right side, so to break a formula of the form "X → Y" you need a row where X is true and Y is false.
```

Check each option with the row most likely to break it:

| Option | Looking for a breaking row | Found? |
|---|---|---|
| A | Needs both disjuncts false. p → q is false only for p true, q false, and then q → p is true | None |
| B | p false, q true: left side true, right side false | Yes |
| C | Needs q false with both premises true, but p true and q false makes p → q false | None |
| D | p false, q true: both premises true, conclusion false | Yes |
| E | The premise p ∧ ¬p is never true | None |

A, C and E have no breaking row, so they are tautologies.

questions.prompt: In an incident review someone argues: "If the new deploy is faulty, the error rate rises. The error rate rose. So the new deploy is faulty." What is the status of this argument?

options.explanation: Modus ponens goes from p → q and **p** to q. Here we are given q and conclude p, which is the reverse.
Modus tollens goes from p → q and ¬q to ¬p. Nothing here is negated.
Correct. From p → q and q you cannot conclude p. The error rate could have risen for another reason, such as a downstream outage.

options.text: Valid, but only if the premise is true
options.explanation: Validity is about form, not about whether the premises happen to be true. This form is invalid even when every premise is true.

questions.workedExample:
1. Let p be "the deploy is faulty" and q be "the error rate rises".
2. Premises: p → q, and q. Conclusion: p.

```formula
p → q, q ⊬ p
where
p: "the new deploy is faulty"
q: "the error rate rises"
→: implies: "if p then q"
,: separates the two premises
⊬: does not follow: some row makes every premise true and the conclusion false
¬: NOT, used in the modus tollens explanation (¬q means "q is false")
In words: knowing that the error rate rose does not tell you the deploy is faulty, because something else could have raised it.
```

3. Search for a row where all premises are true and the conclusion is false (T is true, F is false):

```
p q | p→q  q | p
F T |  T   T | F  <- counterexample
```

4. That row exists, so the argument is invalid. The safe direction is modus tollens: if the error rate did **not** rise, the deploy is not faulty (assuming the premise).

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
xs = []
print(all(x > 0 for x in xs),
      any(x > 0 for x in xs))
```

options.explanation: This treats "all" as needing at least one witness. A universal claim over nothing is vacuously true.
`any` needs at least one element that satisfies the condition. An empty list has none, so `any` is False.
Correct. "Every element is positive" has no element to refute it, so it is vacuously true. "Some element is positive" has no witness, so it is false.

options.text: It raises an exception for an empty iterable
options.explanation: Unlike `max([])`, `all` and `any` are defined on empty iterables: they return their identity values True and False.

questions.workedExample:
1. `all` is a chain of `and`s, and `any` is a chain of `or`s. Each connective has an identity value that changes nothing:

```formula
p ∧ T ≡ p
p ∨ F ≡ p
where
p: any proposition, true or false
∧: AND, what `all` chains together: true only when every part is true
∨: OR, what `any` chains together: true when at least one part is true
T: true, the identity value for AND
F: false, the identity value for OR
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: adding "and true" or "or false" changes nothing, so an empty AND-chain is true and an empty OR-chain is false.
```

2. So `all` of nothing is true, and `any` of nothing is false.
3. In logic terms: "for every x in xs, x > 0" is the implication "if x is in xs then x > 0", whose premise is never true. Vacuous truth.
4. Output: `True False`.

This bites in validation code: `all(check(r) for r in rows)` passes if `rows` is accidentally empty.

questions.prompt:
A policy says: "You may deploy on Friday **only if** you have an approved change ticket." With d = "you deploy on Friday" and t = "you have an approved ticket", which formula captures it?

*Symbols: ∧ means AND; → means "implies" (if ... then); ↔ means "if and only if".*

options.explanation: This says having a ticket forces a deploy. "Only if" names a necessary condition, not a sufficient one; this is the common mix-up.
Correct. "d only if t" means d cannot happen without t: whenever d holds, t holds.
That would be "if and only if". The policy does not say a ticket obliges you to deploy.
That asserts you do deploy and do have a ticket. A policy is a conditional rule, not a statement that the deploy happens.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask: what situation does the policy forbid? Deploying on Friday **without** a ticket: d true, t false.
2. Which formula is false in exactly that row?

```formula
d → t = F   when d = T and t = F
d → t = T   otherwise
where
d: "you deploy on Friday"
t: "you have an approved change ticket"
→: implies: "if d then t", false only when d is true and t is false
↔: if and only if, used in option C: true when both sides have the same truth value
∧: AND, used in option D: true only when both are true
T: true
F: false
In words: d → t forbids exactly the forbidden case, a Friday deploy with no ticket, and allows everything else.
```

3. Check t → d: it is false when t is true and d is false (ticket but no deploy), which the policy allows. Wrong formula.
4. Rule of thumb: "p only if q" means "if p then q", which is p → q.

questions.prompt:
Which formulas are logically equivalent to ¬(p ↔ q)? Select all that apply.

*Symbols: ¬ means NOT; ∧ means AND; ∨ means OR (inclusive); → means "implies" (if ... then); ↔ means "if and only if".*

options.explanation: Correct. p ↔ ¬q is true exactly when p and q differ, which is when p ↔ q is false.
Negating both sides keeps them equal or unequal as before, so this is equivalent to p ↔ q itself, not its negation.
Correct. "At least one, but not both" is exclusive or, which is true exactly when p and q differ.
This is the definition of p ↔ q, not its negation. Confusing a formula with its expansion.

questions.workedExample:
The symbols, and the two expansions you need:

```formula
p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p)
p ⊕ q ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬(p ∧ q)
where
p, q: propositions, each true (T) or false (F)
↔: if and only if: true when p and q have the same truth value
→: implies: false only when the left side is true and the right side false
⊕: XOR (exclusive or): true when exactly one of p, q is true
¬: NOT: flips true and false
∧: AND: true only when both sides are true
∨: OR: true when at least one side is true
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: "p if and only if q" means each implies the other; "exactly one of p, q" means "at least one, but not both".
```

Tabulate (the last column is xor):

```
p q | ¬(p↔q)  p↔¬q  ¬p↔¬q  xor
T T |   F      F     T     F
T F |   T      T     F     T
F T |   T      T     F     T
F F |   F      F     T     F
```

- p ↔ ¬q matches column 1.
- (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬(p ∧ q) is xor and matches.
- ¬p ↔ ¬q is the opposite column.
- (p → q) ∧ (q → p) is p ↔ q, also opposite.

In Python on booleans, all the matching ones are `p != q`.

questions.prompt:
You are building logic from NAND gates only, where p ↑ q ≡ ¬(p ∧ q). Which circuit computes p → q?

*Symbols: ¬ means NOT; ∧ means AND; → means "implies" (if ... then); ≡ means "is logically equivalent to"; ↑ means NAND (not both).*

options.explanation: (p ↑ p) is ¬p, so this is ¬(¬p ∧ q), which is p ∨ ¬q, which is q → p. That is the converse, not p → q.
This NANDs a value with itself, which negates it: ¬¬(p ∧ q) ≡ p ∧ q. It computes AND.
This is ¬(¬p ∧ ¬q), which by De Morgan is p ∨ q. It computes OR.
Correct. (q ↑ q) is ¬q, so this is ¬(p ∧ ¬q), which is ¬p ∨ q, which is p → q.

questions.workedExample:
1. Start from the implication law, rewrite with De Morgan, then turn the negated AND into a NAND:

```formula
p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q
      ≡ ¬(p ∧ ¬q)
      ≡ p ↑ ¬q
      ≡ p ↑ (q ↑ q)
where
p, q: propositions (gate inputs), each true or false
→: implies: false only when p is true and q is false
¬: NOT: flips true and false
∨: OR: true when at least one side is true
∧: AND: true only when both sides are true
↑: NAND (not and): false only when both sides are true
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: "if p then q" is "not (p and not q)", which is p NAND (not q), and not q is q NAND q. Two gates in total.
```

2. Check the failing row, p true and q false (T is true, F is false):

```formula
q ↑ q = F ↑ F = T
p ↑ T = T ↑ T = F
where
p, q: here p = T and q = F
T: true
F: false
↑: NAND: false only when both sides are true
In words: with p true and q false, the circuit outputs false, exactly as p → q should.
```

questions.prompt:
This guard protects the happy path:

```python
if x is not None and x.size > 0:
    process(x)
```

You want an early-return guard for the opposite case. Which condition is **both** logically correct **and** safe to evaluate when `x` is `None`? Assume each non-None x has an ordinary integer size, with no side effects when reading it.

options.text: `if x is None or x.size <= 0: return`
options.explanation: Correct. De Morgan gives ¬a ∨ ¬b, and short-circuit `or` stops after `x is None` is True, so `x.size` is never touched on None.

options.text: `if x.size <= 0 or x is None: return`
options.explanation: Logically equivalent (∨ is commutative), but Python evaluates left to right, so `x.size` raises AttributeError when x is None. Logic ignores evaluation order; code does not.

options.text: `if x is None and x.size <= 0: return`
options.explanation: De Morgan applied without flipping `and` to `or`. It is wrong logically, and it crashes: when x is None it evaluates `x.size`.

options.text: `if x is not None or x.size <= 0: return`
options.explanation: Only the connective was flipped, not the first operand. It returns early for every non-None x, the opposite of what you want.

questions.workedExample:
1. Let a be `x is not None` and b be `x.size > 0`. The guard is a ∧ b.
2. The opposite case is its negation, by De Morgan:

```formula
¬(a ∧ b) ≡ ¬a ∨ ¬b
¬a ∨ ¬b ≡ ¬b ∨ ¬a
where
a: the condition `x is not None`
b: the condition `x.size > 0`
¬: NOT; ¬a is `x is None` and ¬b is `x.size <= 0`
∧: AND (Python `and`)
∨: OR (Python `or`)
≡: is logically equivalent to: same truth value in every case
In words: "not (a and b)" is "not a or not b", which is `x is None or x.size <= 0`. In logic the order of an OR doesn't matter, but in Python it does.
```

3. Python's `or` is short-circuit and left to right:
   - `x is None or ...`: if x is None, stop. Safe.
   - `x.size <= 0 or ...`: evaluates `x.size` first. Crash on None.
4. So option A is the only one that is both correct and safe.

questions.prompt:
Every request is served by region A or region B (p ∨ q). If served by A it is logged (p → r). If served by B it is logged (q → r). Is the conclusion "the request is logged" (r) a **valid** consequence of these premises?

*Symbols: ∨ means OR (inclusive); → means "implies" (if ... then).*

options.text: No: we don't know which region served it, so we can't conclude r
options.explanation: You don't need to know which disjunct holds; both cases lead to r. This is reasoning by cases.

options.text: Yes: in every row where all three premises are true, r is true
options.explanation: Correct. This form (p ∨ q, p → r, q → r ⊢ r) is valid. It is the logic behind proof by cases.

options.text: Only if exactly one region serves each request
options.explanation: ∨ is inclusive and the argument works even if both p and q are true; r follows either way.

options.text: No: this is affirming the consequent
options.explanation: Affirming the consequent concludes p from p → q and q. Here we conclude the consequent r, which is the safe direction.

questions.workedExample:
The argument, written out:

```formula
p ∨ q, p → r, q → r ⊢ r
where
p: "region A served the request"
q: "region B served the request"
r: "the request is logged"
∨: OR (inclusive): at least one region served it, possibly both
→: implies: "if ... then ..."
,: separates the premises
⊢: "therefore": the conclusion on the right follows from the premises on the left
In words: if one of two cases must hold, and each case leads to r, then r holds. This is proof by cases.
```

Look for a row where all premises are true but r is false. If r is false:

```
p → r is T only if p = F
q → r is T only if q = F
then p ∨ q = F  (premise fails)
```

So whenever r is false, at least one premise is false. No counterexample exists, so the argument is valid. Equivalently, the formula "((p ∨ q) ∧ (p → r) ∧ (q → r)) → r" is a tautology (∧ is AND).

lessons.title: Predicate logic and quantifiers
lessons.summary: Predicates, domains and the quantifiers ∀ and ∃, how to translate English and code into them, negating and nesting quantifiers correctly, and where they show up in Big-O, Python and SQL.
lessons.body:
Propositional logic cannot say "every user has an email address" without listing every user. It treats each statement as an indivisible true-or-false value, with no way to talk about *things* and their *properties*.

**Predicate logic** (also called first-order logic) adds exactly that: variables that range over objects, properties of those objects, and the words "for all" and "there exists". It is the language most mathematics is written in, and it is what you are really writing when you use `all()`, `any()` or SQL's `EXISTS`.

## Predicates and domains

A **predicate** is a statement with variables, which becomes a proposition once you plug in values.

- Even(x): "x is even".
- Admin(u): "user u is an admin".
- Less(x, y): "x is less than y", a predicate of two variables.

Plugging in a value gives a plain true-or-false proposition:

```formula
Even(4) = T
Even(7) = F
Less(2, 5) = T
where
Even(x): the predicate "x is even", for a whole number x
Less(x, y): the predicate "x is less than y", for numbers x and y
x, y: variables: placeholders for values from the domain
T: true
F: false
In words: a predicate is a function from values to true or false. "4 is even" is true, "7 is even" is false, "2 is less than 5" is true.
```

Every variable ranges over a **domain** (or **universe of discourse**): the set of things it may stand for. The domain is part of the meaning. "There is a number whose square is 2" is true over the real numbers (the square root of 2, about 1.414) and false over the integers.

## The two quantifiers

Two symbols turn a predicate into a proposition about the whole domain:

```formula
∀x P(x)
∃x P(x)
where
x: a variable ranging over the domain D
D: the domain, the set of things x may stand for
P(x): a predicate: a statement about x that is true or false once x is fixed
∀: "for all", the universal quantifier. ∀x P(x) is true when P(x) is true for every x in D
∃: "there exists", the existential quantifier. ∃x P(x) is true when P(x) is true for at least one x in D
In words: "P holds for every x" and "P holds for at least one x". The symbols are an upside-down A (for "All") and a backwards E (for "Exists").
```

| Symbol | Name | Meaning | Python |
|---|---|---|---|
| ∀x P(x) | universal | P holds for every x | `all(P(x) for x in D)` |
| ∃x P(x) | existential | P holds for at least one x | `any(P(x) for x in D)` |

The Python analogy assumes finite iterables, terminating predicates and no side effects. On a finite domain {d₁, d₂, d₃}, the quantifiers are just big connectives:

```formula
∀x P(x) ≡ P(d_1) ∧ P(d_2) ∧ P(d_3)
∃x P(x) ≡ P(d_1) ∨ P(d_2) ∨ P(d_3)
where
d_1, d_2, d_3: the three members of the domain
x: a variable ranging over that domain
P(x): a predicate, true or false for each x
∀: for all: every member of the domain
∃: there exists: at least one member of the domain
∧: AND: true only when every part is true
∨: OR: true when at least one part is true
≡: is logically equivalent to: always has the same truth value
In words: on a finite domain, "for all" is a long AND over every member, and "there exists" is a long OR.
```

Standard first-order structures usually require a nonempty universe. Restricted quantification over an empty subset is still meaningful; the same conventions apply if empty universes are explicitly allowed. That explains the empty-set behaviour. An empty AND is true and an empty OR is false, so over an empty domain every ∀ statement is (vacuously) true and every ∃ statement is false. `all([])` is `True` and `any([])` is `False` for exactly this reason.

To **disprove** a ∀ claim you need one **counterexample**. To **prove** an ∃ claim you need one **witness**. Proving a ∀ claim over an infinite domain, or disproving an ∃ claim, needs an actual argument; that is what the next lessons are about.

## Translating English

Most real statements quantify over *some* of the domain: "every admin", "some order". These **restricted quantifiers** have a fixed shape, and getting it wrong is the most common error in the whole subject. Over a domain of users:

```formula
∀u (Admin(u) → Verified(u))
∃u (Admin(u) ∧ Verified(u))
where
u: a variable ranging over all users
Admin(u): the predicate "u is an admin"
Verified(u): the predicate "u is verified"
∀: for all users
∃: there exists at least one user
→: implies: "if ... then ...", false only when the left side is true and the right side false
∧: AND: true only when both sides are true
In words: "every user, if an admin, is verified" (every admin is verified) and "some user is both an admin and verified" (some admin is verified).
```

The four common patterns (¬ is NOT):

| English | Formula |
|---|---|
| Every admin is verified | ∀u (Admin(u) → Verified(u)) |
| Some admin is verified | ∃u (Admin(u) ∧ Verified(u)) |
| No admin is verified | ∀u (Admin(u) → ¬Verified(u)) |
| Not every admin is verified | ∃u (Admin(u) ∧ ¬Verified(u)) |

For these restricted-domain translations, use implication under ∀ and conjunction under ∃. This is not a restriction on which connectives may appear in quantified formulas.

> [!warning] The two classic mistranslations
> - ∀u (Admin(u) ∧ Verified(u)) says *everyone* is an admin and verified. Far too strong.
> - ∃u (Admin(u) → Verified(u)) is true as soon as there is a single non-admin, because the implication is then vacuously true. Far too weak.

In code the same shapes appear naturally:

```python
# every admin is verified
all(u.verified for u in users
    if u.admin)

# some admin is verified
any(u.admin and u.verified
    for u in users)
```

The `if` filter in a comprehension plays the role of the →.

## Negating quantifiers

Negation swaps the quantifier and pushes the ¬ inside. These are De Morgan's laws for quantifiers.

```formula
¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x)
¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x)
where
x: a variable ranging over the domain
P(x): a predicate, true or false for each x
¬: NOT: negates whatever follows it
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: "not everything has P" means "something lacks P", and "nothing has P" means "everything lacks P".
```

"Not every test passed" means "some test did not pass"; skipped or pending tests are not automatically failed tests. "No test failed" means "every test did not fail".

With a restricted quantifier, combine this with the rule from the first lesson that "not (if p then q)" is "p and not q":

```formula
¬∀x (A(x) → B(x))
  ≡ ∃x ¬(A(x) → B(x))
  ≡ ∃x (A(x) ∧ ¬B(x))
where
x: a variable ranging over the domain
A(x), B(x): predicates, true or false for each x
¬: NOT
→: implies: false only when the left side is true and the right side false
∧: AND: true only when both sides are true
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: "not every A is a B" means "some A is not a B". The first step flips the quantifier; the second uses the fact that an implication fails exactly when its left side is true and its right side false.
```

> [!example] An SLO, negated
> Hypothetical universal requirement: "every completed request to /checkout takes at most 300 ms". Take r to range over completed requests; the requirement S and its logical negation are below.

```formula
S ≡ ∀r (Checkout(r) → Time(r) ≤ 300)
¬S ≡ ∃r (Checkout(r) ∧ Time(r) > 300)
where
S: the requirement as a single proposition
r: a variable ranging over completed requests
Checkout(r): the predicate "r was a request to /checkout"
Time(r): how long request r took, in milliseconds (ms)
≤: is at most (less than or equal to)
>: is more than
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
→: implies
∧: AND
¬: NOT
≡: is logically equivalent to (here, "is defined as")
In words: the requirement fails exactly when some checkout request took more than 300 ms.
```

One slow completed request refutes this universal requirement. Real SLOs commonly allow an error budget; this is not a recommendation to page on every slow request. Note that ≤ flips to >, not to <.

## Nested quantifiers

Statements with several variables need several quantifiers, and their **order matters** when they are of different kinds.

Let the domain be people and L(x, y) mean "x trusts y".

- ∀x ∃y L(x, y): everyone trusts somebody (possibly different people).
- ∃y ∀x L(x, y): there is one person whom everyone trusts.

The second is much stronger. It implies the first, but not the other way round:

```formula
∃y ∀x L(x, y)  ⊨  ∀x ∃y L(x, y)
∀x ∃y L(x, y)  ⊭  ∃y ∀x L(x, y)
where
x, y: variables ranging over people
L(x, y): the predicate "x trusts y"
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
⊨: logically implies: in every domain and interpretation where the left side is true, the right side is true too
⊭: does not logically imply: some interpretation makes the left side true and the right side false
In words: if one person is trusted by everyone, then everyone trusts somebody. But everyone trusting somebody does not mean there is one person trusted by all.
```

A counterexample to the second line, over the integers with "y > x" in place of L(x, y):

```formula
∀x ∃y (y > x)
y = x + 1
∃y ∀x (y > x)
where
x, y: variables ranging over the integers (…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …)
>: is greater than
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
In words: "every integer has a bigger one" is true, because y = x + 1 is a witness for each x. "Some integer is bigger than every integer" is false: it would need a largest integer.
```

Quantifiers of the **same** kind commute (can swap places):

```formula
∀x ∀y P(x, y) ≡ ∀y ∀x P(x, y)
∃x ∃y P(x, y) ≡ ∃y ∃x P(x, y)
where
x, y: variables ranging over the domain
P(x, y): a predicate of two variables
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: two "for all"s, or two "there exists"es, can be written in either order. Only mixed pairs are order-sensitive.
```

Nested quantifiers are nested loops:

```python
xs = [3, 1, 2]

# ∀x ∃y: y > x ?
print(all(any(y > x for y in xs)
          for x in xs))     # False

# ∃y ∀x: y >= x ?
print(any(all(y >= x for x in xs)
          for y in xs))     # True
```

The first fails at x = 3, since nothing in the list exceeds it. The second succeeds with the witness y = 3.

To negate a nested statement, walk left to right, flipping each quantifier, then negate the inside:

```formula
¬∀x ∃y P(x, y)
  ≡ ∃x ¬∃y P(x, y)
  ≡ ∃x ∀y ¬P(x, y)
where
x, y: variables ranging over the domain
P(x, y): a predicate of two variables
¬: NOT
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: "not everyone has someone they P" means "someone has nobody they P". Each step moves the ¬ one quantifier to the right and flips that quantifier.
```

## A real definition: Big-O

You have already met a nested-quantifier statement. For eventually nonnegative functions on natural-number inputs, Big-O is defined like this:

```formula
f(n) = O(g(n))   iff
∃c > 0 ∃n_0 ∀n ≥ n_0 : f(n) ≤ c · g(n)
where
f(n): the function being bounded, e.g. an algorithm's step count for input size n
g(n): the comparison function, e.g. n or n^2
n: the input size, a natural number (0, 1, 2, …)
O(g(n)): "Big-O of g": grows no faster than a constant times g, once n is large enough
c: a positive constant multiplier, chosen by the prover
n_0: a threshold input size, chosen by the prover; the inequality only has to hold from n_0 upwards
∃: there exists at least one
∀: for all
≥, ≤: is at least, is at most
·: multiplied by
:: "such that" (separates the quantifiers from the condition)
In words: f is O(g) when you can pick a constant c and a starting point n_0 so that, for every n from n_0 on, f(n) is at most c times g(n).
```

Read it as a game. You choose a constant c and a threshold n₀; then any n beyond n₀ must satisfy the inequality.

To show 3n + 10 = O(n), give witnesses: c = 4 and n₀ = 10.

```formula
3 × n + 10 ≤ 3 × n + n = 4 × n   for n ≥ 10
c = 4,  n_0 = 10
where
n: the input size; from n_0 = 10 on, 10 is at most n
c: the constant multiplier chosen as a witness
n_0: the threshold chosen as a witness
≤: is at most
In words: once n is at least 10, the "+ 10" is no bigger than another n, so 3n + 10 is at most 4n. That is the definition with c = 4 and n_0 = 10.
```

To show n² is **not** O(n), prove the negation of the definition (every quantifier flips and ≤ becomes >):

```formula
∀c > 0 ∀n_0 ∃n ≥ n_0 : n^2 > c · n
where
c: any positive constant the opponent picks
n_0: any threshold the opponent picks
n: an input size you must find, at or beyond n_0
n^2: n multiplied by itself
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
·: multiplied by
:: "such that"
In words: whatever constant and threshold are chosen, you can always find a larger input where n² beats c times n.
```

Here is how to find that n for any given c and n₀:

```formula
n = max(n_0, ⌊c⌋ + 1)
n > c
n^2 = n · n > c · n
where
n: the input size you pick
n_0, c: the threshold and constant you were given
max(a, b): the larger of a and b, so n is at least n_0
⌊c⌋: the floor of c: c rounded down to a whole number (⌊2.7⌋ = 2), so ⌊c⌋ + 1 is bigger than c
·: multiplied by
In words: pick n at least n_0 and bigger than c. Then n times n is bigger than c times n. For example, with c = 2.7 and n_0 = 1, n = 3 gives 9 > 8.1.
```

Negating the definition tells you exactly what you have to show.

## Quantifiers and connectives

Some laws let you split quantified statements; some look similar but only hold in one direction:

```formula
∀x (P(x) ∧ Q(x)) ≡ ∀x P(x) ∧ ∀x Q(x)
∃x (P(x) ∨ Q(x)) ≡ ∃x P(x) ∨ ∃x Q(x)
∀x P(x) ∨ ∀x Q(x) ⊨ ∀x (P(x) ∨ Q(x))
∃x (P(x) ∧ Q(x)) ⊨ ∃x P(x) ∧ ∃x Q(x)
where
x: a variable ranging over the domain
P(x), Q(x): predicates, true or false for each x
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
∧: AND
∨: OR
≡: is logically equivalent to (holds both ways)
⊨: logically implies (holds left to right only)
In words: "for all" splits over AND and "there exists" splits over OR, in both directions. "For all" over OR and "there exists" over AND only work one way.
```

Why not the reverse of the last two? Over the integers:

```formula
∀x (Even(x) ∨ Odd(x)) = T
∀x Even(x) ∨ ∀x Odd(x) = F
where
x: a variable ranging over the integers
Even(x): "x is even"
Odd(x): "x is odd"
∀: for all
∨: OR
T: true
F: false
In words: every integer is even or odd, but it is false that every integer is even, and false that every integer is odd.
```

Similarly, there is an even number and there is an odd number, but no number is both, so the ∃-over-AND law can't be reversed either.

## Free and bound variables

In the formula below, the quantifier **binds** x, while y is left **free**:

```formula
∀x (x > y)
∀x P(x) ≡ ∀z P(z)
where
x, z: bound variables: each belongs to the quantifier in front of it, like a loop variable
y: a free variable: nothing quantifies it, so its value must come from outside
P: any predicate
>: is greater than
∀: for all
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: "every x is bigger than y" depends on what y is, so it is a predicate of y, not a proposition. Renaming a bound variable (x to z) changes nothing.
```

A formula with free variables is a predicate, not a proposition: its truth depends on y.

A bound variable is like a loop variable or a function parameter. Renaming it consistently to a fresh name, without capturing a free variable, changes nothing. Reusing the same name in nested scopes is legal but confusing, exactly as shadowing is in code.

## Quantifiers in SQL

SQL has existence tests through EXISTS and quantified comparisons through ALL. It has no standalone FOR ALL quantifier for arbitrary predicates, so universal queries use the negation law:

```formula
∀x P(x) ≡ ¬∃x ¬P(x)
where
x: a variable ranging over the domain (here, rows of a table)
P(x): a predicate, true or false for each x
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one (SQL `EXISTS`)
¬: NOT (SQL `NOT`)
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: "everything has P" means "there is nothing without P".
```

"Customers who have ordered **every** product" becomes a double `NOT EXISTS`:

```formula
∀p ∃o Ord(c, p, o)
  ≡ ¬∃p ¬∃o Ord(c, p, o)
where
c: the customer being tested
p: a variable ranging over products
o: a variable ranging over orders
Ord(c, p, o): the predicate "o is an order by customer c for product p"
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
¬: NOT
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: "c ordered every product" means "there is no product that c has no order for".
```

```sql
SELECT c.id FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM products p
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
      AND o.product_id = p.id));
```

This pattern is called **relational division**. If the products table is empty, every customer is returned: vacuous truth again.

## How far can you automate it?

For propositional logic, you can always decide whether a formula is valid by checking every row (slowly). First-order logic is different. Church and Turing proved in 1936 that no algorithm can decide validity for every first-order formula. Gödel's completeness theorem (1929) says every valid formula has a proof, so you can *search* for proofs, but the search may run forever on a formula that is not valid.

In practice, tools such as Z3 and the Dafny verifier handle large, useful parts of it automatically. The undecidability shows up as timeouts and "unknown" answers, especially around quantifiers.

## Key takeaways
- A predicate becomes a proposition once its variables are fixed; the domain is part of the meaning.
- ∀ (for all) is a big AND and ∃ (there exists) is a big OR; over an empty domain ∀ is true and ∃ is false.
- Restricted quantifiers: ∀ pairs with →, ∃ pairs with ∧.
- ¬∀x P ≡ ∃x ¬P and ¬∃x P ≡ ∀x ¬P; to negate nested quantifiers, flip each one left to right.
- ∃y ∀x is stronger than ∀x ∃y; mixed quantifiers cannot be swapped.
- Big-O, SLOs and SQL's double NOT EXISTS are all quantified statements in disguise.

lessons.title: Proof techniques (direct, contrapositive, contradiction)
lessons.summary: How to prove a claim rather than test it, using direct proof, contrapositive, contradiction and cases, plus existence proofs, counterexamples and the mistakes that make a proof worthless.
lessons.body:
Tests show that code works on the inputs you tried. A **mathematical proof** shows that a claim holds for *every* input, including the ones nobody thought of. Euler's polynomial is the classic warning:

```formula
E(n) = n^2 + n + 41
E(39) = 1521 + 39 + 41 = 1601
E(40) = 1600 + 40 + 41 = 1681 = 41 × 41
where
E(n): Euler's polynomial evaluated at n
n: a natural number (0, 1, 2, …)
n^2: n multiplied by itself
In words: E(n) is prime for every n from 0 to 39 (1601 is prime), but at n = 40 it is 41 × 41, which is not prime.
```

Forty passing tests, one false claim.

Engineers need proofs more often than they expect: to convince yourself an algorithm is correct, that a lower bound is real, that an optimisation is safe, or that a distributed protocol cannot lose data. This lesson covers the main techniques. Almost every proof you will meet is built from them.

## Start with definitions

Most proof failures start with a vague definition. A proof can only use what a term precisely means. Here are the definitions this lesson relies on, written as equations:

```formula
n = 2 × k
n = 2 × k + 1
b = a × k
r = a / b,   b ≠ 0
where
n: a whole number (an integer) being described
k: some integer, which the definition says exists. The first line says n is even, the second that n is odd
a, b: integers. In the third line "b = a × k for some integer k" is what "a divides b" means, written a ∣ b
∣: "divides": a ∣ b means b is a whole-number multiple of a (3 ∣ 12 because 12 = 3 × 4)
r: a number. The fourth line, with integers a and b, says r is rational (a fraction of whole numbers)
≠: is not equal to
In words: even means "twice some integer", odd means "twice some integer, plus one", a divides b means "b is a times some integer", and rational means "an integer over a non-zero integer".
```

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| n is even | n = 2k for some integer k |
| n is odd | n = 2k + 1 for some integer k |
| a ∣ b (a divides b) | b = a·k for some integer k |
| r is rational | r = a/b, integers a, b, b ≠ 0 |
| p is prime | integer p > 1, only positive divisors 1 and p |

(In the table, 2k and a·k mean 2 × k and a × k.) Every integer is either even or odd, and not both. We will use that fact freely.

## Direct proof

To prove an implication "if p then q" (written p → q) directly: **assume p, then derive q** step by step, using definitions and previously proven facts.

**Claim: the sum of two odd integers is even.** Assume m and n are odd. Write each one using the definition of odd, then add them:

```formula
m = 2 × a + 1
n = 2 × b + 1
m + n = (2 × a + 1) + (2 × b + 1)
      = 2 × a + 2 × b + 2
      = 2 × (a + b + 1)
where
m, n: the two odd integers
a, b: integers with m = 2 × a + 1 and n = 2 × b + 1 (they exist because m and n are odd)
In words: the sum is 2 times the integer a + b + 1, which is exactly the definition of even.
```

Since a + b + 1 is an integer, m + n is even. ∎ (The symbol ∎ marks the end of a proof.)

Note what the proof does *not* do: it never picks specific numbers. "3 + 5 = 8 is even" is an example, not a proof. The variables a and b stand for every possible case at once.

A second example, about divisibility, shows the same pattern of unpacking definitions. **Claim: if a divides b and b divides c, then a divides c.** Write both assumptions using the definition of divides, then substitute the first into the second:

```formula
b = a × j
c = b × k
  = (a × j) × k
  = a × (j × k)
where
a, b, c: integers, with a ∣ b and b ∣ c assumed
∣: divides: x ∣ y means y = x × (some integer)
j: the integer with b = a × j (it exists because a ∣ b)
k: the integer with c = b × k (it exists because b ∣ c)
In words: c is a times the integer j × k, so by definition a divides c. For example 2 ∣ 6 and 6 ∣ 18 give 18 = 2 × 9.
```

Since j·k is an integer, a ∣ c. ∎

The recipe: write down what you are given, using definitions. Write down what you need to reach, using definitions. Then close the gap with algebra.

## Proof by contrapositive

Recall from the first lesson that an implication and its contrapositive are logically equivalent:

```formula
p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p
where
p, q: propositions (statements that are true or false)
→: implies: "if ... then ...", false only when the left side is true and the right side false
¬: NOT: ¬q is true exactly when q is false
≡: is logically equivalent to: true in exactly the same situations
In words: "if p then q" says the same as "if not q then not p", so proving either one proves the other.
```

So instead of proving p → q, you may prove ¬q → ¬p directly. This helps when ¬q gives you something concrete to work with and p does not.

**Claim: if n² (n squared) is even, then n is even.** A direct attempt starts with "n² is twice some integer" and needs a square root, which goes nowhere. The contrapositive is: if n is **odd**, then n² is **odd**. So write n using the definition of odd and square it:

```formula
n = 2 × k + 1
n^2 = (2 × k + 1)^2
    = 4 × k^2 + 4 × k + 1
    = 2 × (2 × k^2 + 2 × k) + 1
where
n: an odd integer
k: the integer with n = 2 × k + 1
n^2: n multiplied by itself (n squared)
In words: n² is 2 times an integer, plus 1, so it is odd. With n = 7 (k = 3): 49 = 2 × 24 + 1.
```

So n odd forces n² odd, which proves the claim. ∎

Another one, where the contrapositive turns an awkward "or" into a clean "and". **Claim: if two numbers add up to at least 100, at least one of them is at least 50.** In symbols, with the contrapositive below it:

```formula
x + y ≥ 100  →  x ≥ 50 or y ≥ 50
x < 50 and y < 50  →  x + y < 100
x + y < 50 + 50 = 100
where
→: implies: "if the left side holds, then the right side holds"
x, y: real numbers
≥: is greater than or equal to
<: is less than
In words: the first line is the claim and the second its contrapositive. The third line proves the contrapositive: two numbers that are each under 50 add up to less than 100. So if the sum reaches 100, at least one of them must be 50 or more.
```

This is the pigeonhole principle in miniature. The same reasoning appears in capacity planning: if two shards each hold under half the keys, they cannot together hold them all.

## Proof by contradiction

To prove a statement S: **assume ¬S (not S) and derive something impossible**, such as a statement and its negation. Since a true assumption cannot lead to a false conclusion, ¬S must be false, so S is true.

The two classic examples are over 2,000 years old.

### √2 is irrational

Suppose the square root of 2 is rational. Then it is a fraction a/b of integers with b ≠ 0, and we may take the fraction in lowest terms (a and b share no factor, as any fraction can be reduced). Square both sides and rearrange:

```formula
√2 = a / b
2 = a^2 / b^2
a^2 = 2 × b^2
where
√2: the square root of 2, the positive number whose square is 2 (about 1.41421)
a, b: integers with no common factor, b ≠ 0, assumed to satisfy √2 = a / b
a^2, b^2: a and b squared
≠: is not equal to
In words: if √2 were a fraction a/b, then a² would be exactly twice b², so a² would be even.
```

So a² is even, which means a is even (that is the contrapositive result above). Write a = 2k and substitute:

```formula
(2 × k)^2 = 2 × b^2
4 × k^2 = 2 × b^2
b^2 = 2 × k^2
where
k: the integer with a = 2 × k
b: the denominator from before
In words: b² is twice an integer, so b² is even, and so b is even too.
```

Now a and b are both even, so a/b is not in lowest terms. Contradiction. ∎

The proof uses the earlier contrapositive result as a **lemma**. Building proofs from smaller proven pieces is like building programs from tested functions.

### There are infinitely many primes (Euclid)

Suppose there are only finitely many primes, and list them all as p₁, p₂, …, pₖ. Build a new number N from them:

```formula
N = p_1 × p_2 × ... × p_k + 1
N − p_1 × p_2 × ... × p_k = 1
where
N: the product of every listed prime, plus 1
p_1, p_2, ..., p_k: the supposedly complete list of primes
k: how many primes are on the list
...: and so on, through every prime on the list
In words: N is one more than the product of all the primes, so subtracting that product from N leaves exactly 1.
```

N > 1, so N has a prime factor q. Since the list is supposed to be complete, q is one of the pᵢ, so q divides the product p₁·p₂·…·pₖ. q also divides N, so q divides their difference, which is 1. No prime divides 1. Contradiction. ∎

> [!warning] A common misreading
> The proof does **not** say N itself is prime. 2·3·5·7·11·13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 × 509. It says N has a prime factor missing from the list, which is all the contradiction needs.

### Contradiction or contrapositive?

When proving p → q by contradiction, you assume "p and not q" (written p ∧ ¬q, where ∧ is AND) and hunt for any impossibility. A contrapositive proof assumes ¬q and must reach exactly ¬p. If the derivation of ¬p uses only ¬q and background facts, without relying on the additional assumption p, it can be restated as a direct contrapositive proof. Otherwise it remains a contradiction argument.

Contradiction shines when the claim is a negative ("there is no...", "is not rational", "cannot be decided"). In computer science, the proof that the halting problem is undecidable is a proof by contradiction, and contradiction is also useful in many lower-bound arguments.

## Proof by cases

If every possibility falls into one of several cases, prove the claim in each case separately. This is the valid argument form called **proof by cases** (or disjunction elimination):

```formula
p ∨ q, p → r, q → r ⊢ r
where
p, q: the cases, propositions that are true or false
r: the claim being proved
∨: OR (inclusive): at least one case holds
→: implies: "if this case, then the claim"
,: separates the premises
⊢: "therefore": the conclusion on the right follows from the premises on the left
In words: if one of the cases must hold, and each case leads to r, then r holds.
```

**Claim: no sum of two squares leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4.** First, squares mod 4 (the remainder after dividing by 4). Every integer n is even or odd, which gives two cases:

```formula
n = 2 × k:      n^2 = 4 × k^2
n = 2 × k + 1:  n^2 = 4 × (k^2 + k) + 1
where
n: any integer
k: the integer from the definition of even (first line) or odd (second line)
n^2: n squared
In words: an even number's square is a multiple of 4 (remainder 0), and an odd number's square is a multiple of 4 plus 1 (remainder 1).
```

So any square leaves remainder 0 or 1. A sum a² + b² of two squares leaves 0 + 0, 0 + 1 or 1 + 1, that is 0, 1 or 2. Never 3. ∎

So 7, 11, 15, 19, ... can never be written as a sum of two squares. A bounded search over many target integers would not prove the universal claim. For one fixed nonnegative target, exhaustive search over bounded candidate squares can prove that target has no representation; the case split handles all targets at once.

The cases must be **exhaustive**. Forgetting a case (zero, negatives, the empty list) is the proof equivalent of a missing branch in code.

## If and only if

To prove "p if and only if q" (written p ↔ q), prove both directions: p → q **and** q → p. They often need different techniques.

**Claim: n is even if and only if n² is even.** Forwards (→): if n = 2k, then n² is twice an integer:

```formula
n^2 = (2 × k)^2 = 4 × k^2 = 2 × (2 × k^2)
where
n: an even integer, n = 2 × k
k: an integer
n^2: n squared
In words: the square of an even number is 2 times an integer, so it is even.
```

Backwards (←): if n² is even then n is even, which we proved above by contrapositive. Both directions hold. ∎

A common slip is proving one direction twice, once forwards and once by its contrapositive, which proves only one implication.

## Existence proofs and counterexamples

To prove "there exists an x with property P" (written ∃x P(x)), the most convincing approach is **constructive**: exhibit a specific x and check it.

Sometimes you can prove existence without saying which object works. A famous **non-constructive** proof. **Claim: there exist irrational numbers a and b with aᵇ rational.** Let x = √2 raised to the power √2. Either x is rational or it is not.

- If x is rational, take a = b = √2: both irrational, and aᵇ = x is rational.
- If x is irrational, take a = x and b = √2, and compute:

```formula
x = √2^√2
a^b = (√2^√2)^√2
    = √2^(√2 × √2)
    = √2^2 = 2
where
√2: the square root of 2, about 1.41421, which is irrational
x: √2 raised to the power √2, about 1.63
a, b: the candidate pair, here a = x and b = √2
a^b: a raised to the power b
In words: raising √2^√2 to the power √2 multiplies the exponents, giving √2 squared, which is 2, a rational number.
```

Either way such a and b exist. ∎

The proof is valid, yet it doesn't tell you which case holds. (x is in fact irrational, by the Gelfond–Schneider theorem, but the proof doesn't need that.)

To **disprove** a "for all" claim (written ∀x P(x)), a single **counterexample** is enough, as n = 40 is for Euler's polynomial. Checking finitely many examples does not prove a universal claim over an infinite domain. Exhaustively checking every case in a known finite domain can prove it; a counterexample disproves either kind of universal claim.

## How proofs go wrong

| Mistake | What happens |
|---|---|
| Incomplete proof by examples | Leaves unchecked cases unjustified |
| Proving the converse | Shows "if q then p", not "if p then q" |
| Assuming the goal | Circular reasoning |
| Hidden division by 0 | Any "result" follows |
| Missing cases | Gap where the claim may fail |

The classic fake proof that 2 = 1 hides a division by zero. Start with a = b = 1:

```formula
a^2 = a × b
a^2 − b^2 = a × b − b^2
(a + b) × (a − b) = b × (a − b)
a + b = b
2 × b = b
2 = 1
where
a, b: two numbers, both set to 1
a^2, b^2: a and b squared
In words: every line up to the third is true. The fourth line cancels the factor (a − b) from both sides, which is dividing by a − b = 0, and from there on every line is false.
```

Since a = b, the step that cancels (a − b) divides by zero. Every line before it is true; the line after is not.

> [!tip] A template that avoids most errors
> 1. State the claim precisely, with quantifiers.
> 2. Say which technique you are using.
> 3. Write down the assumptions, expanded using definitions.
> 4. Write down the goal, expanded the same way.
> 5. Bridge the gap, justifying each step.
> 6. Say clearly where the proof ends.

## Key takeaways
- A proof covers every case under its assumptions. Partial sampling gives evidence; exhaustive finite checking can prove a finite-domain claim. One counterexample refutes a universal claim.
- Unpack definitions (even = 2k, a ∣ b means b = ak) before doing anything clever.
- Direct: assume p, derive q. Contrapositive: assume ¬q, derive ¬p. Contradiction: assume ¬S, derive something impossible.
- Case splits must be exhaustive; "if and only if" needs both directions.
- Existence can be shown constructively (give the object) or non-constructively.
- Watch for circular reasoning, proving the converse and hidden division by zero.

questions.workedExample:
1. Hypothesis: n is odd. By definition, n = 2k + 1 for some integer k.
2. Goal: n² is odd, that is, n² = 2m + 1 for some integer m.
3. Bridge the gap with algebra:

```formula
n = 2 × k + 1
n^2 = (2 × k + 1)^2
    = 4 × k^2 + 4 × k + 1
    = 2 × (2 × k^2 + 2 × k) + 1
m = 2 × k^2 + 2 × k
where

k: the integer with n = 2 × k + 1
```

```formula
where
p: "n² is odd" (n² is n squared)
```
